          "questions": "Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems often struggle with reward specification: it is notoriously difficult to craft a reward function that captures the intended goals in all scenarios, so designers rely on proxy rewards that only approximate the true objective. Agents that optimize such imperfect proxies can discover unintended, exploitative behaviors that achieve high proxy return while yielding poor true outcomes, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. Reward hacking is not merely hypothetical: it has led to undesirable or even catastrophic consequences in safety-critical settings and is common in real-world deployments. At the same time, interpretability and transparency of RL policies are increasingly recognized as requirements for real-world acceptance: policymakers and practitioners in safety-critical domains need systems that are not only robust but also understandable, so that they can identify which decision-making criteria lead to undesirable outcomes, mitigate risks, and ensure compliance with safety regulations. RL algorithms for high-stakes applications therefore face two fundamental challenges: robustness to uncertain or poorly specified rewards, and interpretability that facilitates oversight by human stakeholders.\n\nRecent work has begun to formalize reward hacking and to develop principled mitigations. In one such framework, the agent is given a proxy reward and a reference policy, while the true reward is hidden. The proxy is called r-correlated with the true reward if the two maintain a correlation coefficient r > 0 on the state-action pairs encountered by the reference policy, that is, under the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. This definition permits the proxy and the true reward to diverge arbitrarily in parts of the state-action space that the reference policy does not visit, which are precisely the regions an RL agent may exploit under intensive optimization. Reward hacking is then said to occur when optimizing an r-correlated proxy yields a policy with lower true reward than the reference policy. The mitigation proposed within that framework, Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO), augments the standard RL objective with a regularization term that penalizes the chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, with a strength that depends on the correlation level, and it guarantees a lower bound on the improvement in true reward.\n\nDespite this progress, existing solutions to reward hacking have several limitations. First, their effectiveness relies heavily on the specific proxy reward. Designing good proxies is hard: in real-world scenarios, proxies are often derived heuristically or empirically from noisy or limited data, which leaves uncertainty about their exact relationship to the true reward, and the correlation level itself is typically known only approximately. Robustness to variations in the proxy is therefore crucial for dependable deployment, yet a method that regularizes against one fixed proxy offers only a weak guarantee on worst-case performance when the proxy could be any reward consistent with the assumed correlation, including an adversarially chosen one. Second, current methods treat the reward function as a black box and learn complex policies with no easily interpretable structure, making it hard to understand why a policy avoids reward hacking or to trust its behavior in novel situations; moreover, they cannot easily incorporate prior knowledge about the true reward when such knowledge is available.\n\nThis raises several research questions. Given only a proxy reward, a reference policy and an assumed correlation level, how can one learn a policy whose true performance is guaranteed against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint, rather than against a single trusted proxy? Can such a guarantee be turned into an objective that is tractable to optimize with standard policy-optimization tools? How should state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits, where the correlation constraint says nothing about the true reward, be handled? When prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward is available, how can it be exploited to avoid excessive conservatism and to expose, in an interpretable way, which aspects of the reward a learned policy is most vulnerable to? Finally, how can one obtain policies whose performance remains robust and stable when the true correlation between proxy and true reward is uncertain or misspecified?",

          "questions": "The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.\n\nMost current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.\n\nThe gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.",

          "questions": "Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.\n\nMethods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.\n\nAlthough diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.\n\nThese failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.\n\nA further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.\n\nThis raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?",

          "questions": "Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.\n\nAmong the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.\n\nTwo representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.\n\nDistributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.\n\nThe problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure.           "questions": "Spatiotemporal partial differential equations (PDEs) are the foundation for modeling dynamical systems across science and engineering, governing phenomena in fluid dynamics, weather forecasting, molecular dynamics and energy systems, and solving them accurately is crucial for scientific discovery and engineering design. Classical numerical solvers can provide reliable solutions, but they often become computationally prohibitive for large-scale problems on irregular domains, which are common in scientific and engineering applications. Neural PDE solvers have therefore emerged as a promising alternative that approximates solution operators directly from data. In practice, however, high-fidelity PDE data, whether collected from real systems or generated by simulation, are expensive to obtain. Existing neural PDE solvers typically require large numbers of training trajectories to perform well across the solution domain, and their accuracy degrades substantially when data are limited, which indicates low data efficiency. Improving the data efficiency of neural PDE learning therefore remains a critical yet underexplored challenge.\n\nA fundamental reason for this limitation lies in the structural nature of PDE dynamics. PDE systems embody strong physical and mathematical inductive biases, such as locality, conservation laws and superposition, that govern how states evolve over space and time, yet most neural architectures do not encode these structural priors explicitly, or incorporate them only weakly. Physics-informed neural networks add PDE residuals and boundary conditions as soft constraints in the training loss, but they essentially learn one solution under a fixed setup, cannot generalize to domains, parameters or forcing terms beyond the training distribution, and need rapidly growing amounts of data when accurate solutions are required across the solution domain. Neural operators such as DeepONet and the Fourier Neural Operator learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces and generalize across resolutions and physical parameters, but they incorporate limited physical structure, and learning operator mappings in function spaces requires substantial amounts of data. Graph-based solvers are a natural backbone for spatiotemporal PDEs on irregular domains, and later works have strengthened their physical consistency by embedding conservation laws, operator blocks or invariants such as momentum conservation; still, they lack a principled structural foundation and rely on substantial data to learn complex physical dynamics. Consequently, models must learn the underlying operator structure and physical constraints directly from data, which leads to high sample complexity and reduced data efficiency.\n\nThe issue becomes particularly pronounced in the presence of source terms, which represent external forcing applied over space and time, such as time-varying heat sources in conduction, body forces in fluid dynamics, time-dependent currents in electromagnetics or seismic excitations in elasticity. Consider a physical state $u(\\mathbf{x}, t)$ governed by $\\partial_t u = \\mathcal{L}_{\\mathbf{x}}[u] + f(\\mathbf{x}, t)$ on a spatial domain $\\Omega$ over a time interval $(0, T]$, where $\\mathcal{L}_{\\mathbf{x}}$ is a spatial differential operator characterizing the system dynamics and $f$ is the source term, and where the evolution is determined by an initial condition and by boundary conditions such as Dirichlet or Neumann conditions. In many real-world systems the source varies substantially across space and time and plays a decisive role in the solution behavior. Training trajectories, however, typically cover only a subset of the possible source patterns, and existing solvers struggle to extrapolate to unseen ones: although current approaches generalize across resolutions, physical parameters or system sizes, a critical gap remains, since none of them can generalize to unseen source terms, even though such varying sources are ubiquitous in practice. Poor generalization to unseen source terms is thus a representative manifestation of insufficient inductive bias and data inefficiency, and generalization to varying source terms is a stringent test of the data efficiency and structural inductive bias of a neural PDE solver.\n\nTo improve data efficiency, stronger structural priors are needed that meaningfully reduce the learning space and exploration burden of neural solvers. This raises the following questions. Which structural properties of PDE dynamics can be encoded explicitly in a neural solver, so that it no longer has to rediscover fundamental physical structure from data? Can a solver built on such priors learn accurate spatiotemporal dynamics on irregular domains with complex geometries and boundary conditions from only a limited number of training trajectories?           "questions": "Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.\n\nTo address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., \"A person is holding a cup\", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.\n\nAt the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.\n\nEffective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?",

          "questions": "Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.\n\nTwo families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.\n\nUsing exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.\n\nThe problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?",

          "questions": "Visual document retrieval is the task of returning relevant documents, typically PDFs containing figures, tables, and other visual elements, in response to a textual query. Neural retrieval pipelines for this task often follow a text-centric approach: source documents are converted into textual chunks with optical character recognition or vision-language models, and an index is then built with semantic text encoders. An alternative, vision-centric approach relies instead on multimodal encoders. Building on the ColBERT late-interaction approach, ColPali-based encoders operate directly on page images, matching textual query tokens to image patches and producing multi-vector embeddings of images and queries.\n\nAlthough this vision-centric paradigm achieves state-of-the-art results on public visual document retrieval benchmarks, open challenges remain. First, in pursuit of state-of-the-art performance, recent late-interaction multimodal retrievers have massively scaled the length and dimensionality of their query and document representations. This incurs substantial latency and storage overhead and hinders efficient, scalable deployment in real-world pipelines; one recent retriever, for example, represents each document page with about 10 MB of memory, three orders of magnitude more than a single-vector dense retriever. Second, matching textual queries to textually rich documents with a purely vision-centric model may be limited by the substantial modality gap that modern vision-language models still exhibit. These limitations motivate exploring complementary ways of improving multimodal encoders, rather than relying only on ever-larger monolithic models.\n\nA long-standing idea in neural retrieval is hybrid retrieval, in which the outputs of different retrievers are aggregated, at the level of document ranks or of query-document similarity scores, to obtain the final list of retrieved documents. Hybrid retrieval (or hybrid search) most commonly refers to combining a neural semantic text retriever with a sparse lexical representation such as BM25; more broadly, it reflects the notion that models relying on different types of representations capture complementary aspects of the data, which can be leveraged to boost overall performance. Dense text retrievers typically have low online latency and a small storage footprint, and they provide a uni-modal signal between the query and the document representation. Combining text and image encoders therefore emerges as a natural candidate for enhancing a multimodal retrieval system.\n\nHowever, standard hybrid retrieval methods take a rather coarse-grained view of each retriever: because they reduce every query-document pair to a single rank or score, they cannot exploit the rich query-document interactions within each model's representation space. Aggregating at the level of the representations themselves would carry the richest information, but at query time it is hindered by heterogeneity: encoders may use a single vector or many vectors per query and document, with differing dimensionalities and scales, and any aggregation must respect strict latency and memory budgets without access to supervision. A further difficulty is that the complementary retriever may be lightweight and even weaker on the task than the primary one, and it is unclear whether such a signal can help at all.\n\nThis raises the following questions. Can the paradigm of hybrid retrieval complement modern vision-centric multimodal encoders, and in particular, can a lightweight dense text retriever enhance a stronger vision-centric retriever? How can the signals of two heterogeneous retrievers be combined at query time so as to exploit the rich interactions within their representation spaces, rather than only their final ranks or scores, while remaining architecture-agnostic (applicable to both single-vector and multi-vector models), lightweight, and practical?           "questions": "Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.\n\nIn continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.\n\nActor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.\n\nThis raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?",

          "questions": "Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).\n\nExisting VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.\n\nThis calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: \"inserting a screw\" or \"aligning parts\" may look alike in tasks such as \"Assemble a chair\" and \"Fix a table\", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.\n\nThe research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?",

          "questions": "Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.\n\nDespite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.\n\nThe gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.\n\nThis raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?",

          "questions": "Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.\n\nYet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.\n\nSo far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.\n\nThis leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.",

          "questions": "Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.\n\nGeneral-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.\n\nRecently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.\n\nIt is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data.           "questions": "Directed graphs (digraphs) model systems with asymmetric relationships, capturing essential structures such as flows, dependencies, and hierarchies that arise in many real-world applications. This makes digraphs particularly well-suited for problems in diverse domains including biology, transportation, social dynamics, and, more recently, image and video understanding, where structured and directional representations are critical for interpretation and reasoning. Consequently, generating digraphs is central to tasks such as simulation, data augmentation and novel instance discovery in domains with directional structure.\n\nGraph generative models aim to learn the probability distribution of a set of observed graphs, enabling the generation of new samples that preserve structural and statistical properties. Such models have shown strong potential in diverse applications, including drug discovery, finance, social network modeling, and medicine. However, most generative models focus on undirected graphs, with only limited efforts on directed settings. The vast majority of works on directed graph generation focus solely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with autoencoders, autoregressive methods and, more recently, diffusion combined with an auto-regressive process; these require the input DAGs to be topologically ordered, which can result in higher computational cost. Other approaches are tailored to specific applications and, therefore, to DAGs. A general digraph generation method, following an auto-regressive perspective, has only recently been proposed, and its implementation is not publicly available, limiting its accessibility for study and evaluation.\n\nTwo main factors limit progress in this direction. First, at the modeling level, the directed setting is inherently more challenging than its undirected counterpart: edge directionality greatly enlarges the learnable space (for graphs with 4 nodes, there are 218 possible digraphs, compared to only 11 undirected ones) and introduces a substantially larger dependency space, making the underlying distribution harder to learn. In directed graphs, a model must distinguish the different semantics carried by incoming and outgoing edges. The difficulty is further amplified in settings where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity in DAGs. Second, beyond these technical challenges, the lack of standardized benchmarks for directed graph generation is a barrier to rigorous evaluation and fair comparison: existing approaches typically rely only on proxy metrics derived from downstream tasks, failing to directly evaluate generative quality, and there are no established benchmarks to evaluate digraph generative quality systematically.\n\nThis raises several questions.           "questions": "Transporting mass between probability distributions is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning and beyond. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled approach to such problems by seeking to minimise the total cost of transportation under a chosen cost function, and computational OT, from Sinkhorn's algorithm to more recent neural approaches, has been applied successfully in domains such as biology and extensively within machine learning. More recently, ideas from the flow-based approaches that have revolutionised generative modelling have been leveraged to solve the entropy-regularised dynamic OT problem known as the Schrödinger bridge (SB): finding the most likely evolution of a population between two prescribed distributions, relative to a reference stochastic process. With a Brownian reference process, the static form of this problem is exactly entropy-regularised OT for the quadratic cost. Flow-based SB solvers offer significant scalability advantages, enabling the approximation of OT maps between high-dimensional continuous datasets such as images. Early flow-based solvers were built on the classical Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) scheme, which preserves both marginals only at convergence, requires expensive caching of simulated trajectories and tends to 'forget' the reference measure; such methods have since been superseded by solvers based on the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, which avoids these issues.\n\nBeyond the standard two-marginal problem, multi-marginal OT seeks a joint coupling over several marginals that minimises a total cost. Tree-structured costs are often considered, as they frequently arise in applications while allowing improved scalability by exploiting the tree structure. In the corresponding tree-structured SB problem, stochastic processes run along the edges of a tree and marginals are prescribed only at a subset of the vertices; with Brownian motion along each edge as the reference, it is an entropy-regularised multi-marginal OT problem with a tree-structured quadratic cost. Star-shaped trees, with marginals fixed on the leaves and an unknown centre, are of particular significance because they correspond to an entropy-regularised form of the Wasserstein barycentre problem. The Wasserstein barycentre provides a natural notion of 'average' for probability distributions and is widely studied because of its importance in applications such as Bayesian learning, clustering and representation learning. Computing barycentres is notoriously challenging. Many successful approaches approximate the solution with a finite set of points, but such in-sample methods struggle to scale as dimensionality increases and cannot generate new samples; alternative methods provide continuous approximations through neural parameterisations, but often require multi-level or adversarial optimisation procedures. To date, the only neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation extends the IPF-based diffusion Schrödinger bridge to the tree-structured SB setting, and therefore inherits the drawbacks of IPF; it has been reported to suffer training instability at low entropic regularisation, struggling to match the prescribed marginals at the vertices.\n\nIn parallel, one of the most successful approaches to Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation is the iterative fixed-point method, which repeatedly updates a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps. It performs strongly and has been observed to converge in only a few iterations, but every iteration requires solving a complete OT problem to each marginal, which is expensive because solving even a single OT problem can be challenging.\n\nThis raises several questions. Can a scalable, flow-based solver be built for the tree-structured SB problem, and hence for entropic Wasserstein barycentres, that avoids the shortcomings of IPF-based schemes while being guaranteed to converge to the tree-structured SB solution? In the barycentre case, can the fast convergence of fixed-point schemes be retained without paying for a complete OT solve to every marginal at every iteration? And can flow-based barycentre solvers of this kind offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation?",

          "questions": "Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.\n\nMetanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.\n\nA major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.\n\nBuilding on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.\n\nRelaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.\n\nThis raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?",

          "questions": "Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.\n\nMore recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.\n\nAn orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.\n\nThe open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?",

          "questions": "Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.\n\nRadio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.\n\nThe open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.\n\nHow can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?",

          "questions": "Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.\n\nThis works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.\n\nIgnoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.\n\nThis raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?",
