          "questions": "Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.\n\nThe task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.\n\nExisting synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.\n\nBuilding a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.\n\nThis raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.",

          "questions": "Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.\n\nParallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.\n\nSeveral obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.\n\nThis raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering?           "questions": "Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.\n\nExisting benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.\n\nExisting editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.\n\nThis raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?",

          "questions": "Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.\n\nAlthough foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as \"Right Eye Close\", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.\n\nExisting facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads.           "questions": "Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.\n\nModality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.\n\nWhile effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.\n\nRobustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.\n\nThis raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?",

          "questions": "Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.\n\nCausal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\\in\\mathbb{R}^{T\\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\\top k_i/\\sqrt{d}$ for $i\\le t$ and $-\\infty$ otherwise, and set $\\alpha_{t,\\cdot}=\\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\\{1,\\dots,t\\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\\sum_{i\\le t}\\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\\{v_1,\\dots,v_t\\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.\n\nThis convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.\n\nMost recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.\n\nThis leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?",

          "questions": "In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.\n\nFormally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.\n\nIn particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.\n\nDetecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.\n\nThe question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.",

          "questions": "Large language models have recently improved their reasoning by spending more test-time compute, generating more tokens before producing a final answer. Extended sequential scaling has limits, however: beyond a certain length, performance can decrease because of \"overthinking\", and long sequential reasoning can be sensitive to the order of reasoning steps. A complementary scaling dimension, repeated parallel sampling followed by aggregation, as in self-consistency (majority voting) or Best-of-N selection, has further boosted reasoning performance. These parallel methods rely on the model generating solutions that are both diverse and correct, and as tasks become harder, some mechanism for increasing diversity becomes necessary.\n\nObtaining such diversity is difficult. Only a minority of tokens in a chain of thought act as forking tokens that lead to distinct reasoning modes, so as problems become harder and generations longer, these tokens become substantially harder to sample. The common practice for encouraging diversity, raising the sampling temperature, inherently entails a diversity-accuracy trade-off, because the forking tokens that trigger diverse yet correct reasoning modes typically lie deep within the sampling tree. Theoretical work further shows that increasing the temperature alone does not necessarily yield greater diversity unless the model has been explicitly trained to ensure coverage. Search-based alternatives such as Monte Carlo tree search or Tree of Thoughts increase coverage through heuristic-guided search with an external verifier, but their reliance on heuristics and domain-specific knowledge limits the tasks to which they apply. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is not a complete answer either: it requires a strong base model, and recent work suggests that it does not by itself instill new capabilities, so what a model learns during fine-tuning matters.\n\nAt the same time, several distinct and correct reasoning traces per question can be obtained at low cost and without human annotation, for instance by distilling from different teacher models, sampling repeatedly, and filtering with a verifiable correctness check. This suggests training models for coverage directly from such diverse traces, but how to do so is unclear. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats each trace as an independent example and has no explicit mechanism for keeping different reasoning modes apart: it is an open question whether the modes are preserved or merged into one, and whether a particular mode can later be deliberately elicited. Recent efforts to train models natively for parallel reasoning, by converting sequential chains of thought into parallel ones or by training on multiple traces distilled from teachers, show that native parallel scaling can surpass sequential scaling within certain token limits, but they leave open whether the distinct reasoning modes present in the training traces are actually retained and can be reliably triggered.\n\nThe problem is therefore how to fine-tune a language model on a set of diverse, correct reasoning traces per question so that it retains their distinct reasoning modes rather than collapsing them, and so that diverse yet accurate reasoning paths can be reliably triggered when sampling in parallel, instead of depending on sampling rare forking tokens deep inside a generation.           "questions": "Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique in machine learning, widely used for model compression, transfer learning, and improving generalization. Its core idea is to transfer knowledge from a \"teacher\" model to a (typically smaller) \"student\" model by training the student to match the teacher's output probabilities rather than categorical one-hot labels. This softened supervision has been shown to improve performance across a range of tasks. Consequently, a substantial body of research has focused on designing distillation mechanisms, such as dynamic temperature scaling, feature-based distillation, and task-aware teacher-student matching, typically assuming a large teacher that is optimized to maximize its own performance.\n\nDespite its widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of knowledge distillation remain only partially understood. In particular, the impact of the teacher's output probabilities on the student's optimization trajectory and generalization has not been fully characterized. Existing explanations attribute the usefulness of distillation to the regularizing effect of the teacher's soft estimates, to trade-offs such as precision versus recall or knowledge inheritance versus exploration, or to factors such as data geometry and optimization bias. Insights into how distillation affects the optimization itself have been developed only for special cases, such as self-distillation or a student that is a compressed version of the teacher, and rely on dedicated gradient approximations. A principled understanding of how distillation affects common learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, for arbitrary teachers, is still lacking.\n\nRecent works have begun to view distillation through a Bayesian lens, interpreting the teacher's outputs as (possibly noisy) estimates of the true class posterior probabilities of the data-generating distribution. From this statistical viewpoint, learning from accurate class posteriors has been argued to reduce the variance of the student's objective, and excess-risk and generalization bounds have been derived in terms of the distance between the teacher's predictions and the true posteriors. These analyses, however, characterize the statistical properties of the risk rather than the behavior of the learning algorithm that actually trains the student. The probabilistic perspective thus opens relatively unexplored questions about the dynamics of SGD-based learning under probabilistic supervision, and about how the statistical calibration of the teacher influences the student. Teacher calibration has been recognized as a key driver of distillation, but it remains unclear how the quality of the teacher's probability estimates should guide the way teachers are built.\n\nThis raises several questions. How does supervising a student with the exact class posterior probabilities, instead of one-hot labels, change the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learning and the generalization of the resulting student? In the realistic case where the teacher provides only imperfect, noisy estimates of these posteriors, how does the level of estimation error affect the student's convergence, generalization and accuracy, and under what conditions does probabilistic supervision remain preferable to one-hot labels? Finally, what practical guidelines follow for designing or choosing teacher models, beyond maximizing the teacher's own accuracy, so that their outputs provide better supervision for students trained with SGD-based optimizers?",

          "questions": "Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.\n\nOne promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.\n\nThese overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.\n\nExisting lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.\n\nThis raises the following questions.           "questions": "Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.\n\nAlthough UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.\n\nStudies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.\n\nThe central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.",

          "questions": "Novel view synthesis is a critical area in computer vision, with applications in scene manipulation, autonomous driving, virtual fly-throughs, and 3D generation models. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have emerged as a leading technology, leveraging implicit scene representations through neural networks and volume rendering to generate novel views. MLP-based radiance fields such as Mip-NeRF360, which significantly improved anti-aliasing and the handling of unbounded scenes, produce high-quality renderings with compact model sizes, but they suffer from slow training and rendering because volume rendering requires extensive querying of the network. Methods that augment NeRF with structured arrays of learnable features, such as compact low-rank tensor decompositions (TensoRF) or multi-resolution hash tables combined with small fully-fused MLPs (Instant-NGP), accelerate training and rendering considerably, yet these grid-based methods still struggle to reach real-time rendering and to match the quality of MLP-based approaches, often because of limited grid resolution or hash collisions.\n\n3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a compelling alternative to NeRF-based approaches, enabling real-time rendering of high-resolution novel views. Instead of continuous neural networks, 3DGS represents a scene with a set of explicit, optimizable 3D Gaussians, each defined by a position, an opacity, a rotation, an anisotropic scale and a color expressed with spherical harmonics; the Gaussians are initialized from Structure-from-Motion points and adaptively densified during optimization. By bypassing the computational overhead of volume rendering through an efficient differentiable point-based splatting process, 3DGS achieves real-time performance while enhancing rendering quality.\n\nHowever, 3DGS suffers from significant memory overhead due to its parameter-intensive representation of view-dependent colors and anisotropic shapes. Each 3D Gaussian requires 59 parameters, with 48 parameters dedicated to view-dependent color via spherical harmonics and 7 parameters encoding anisotropic scale and rotation, so that models built from 3D Gaussians are considerably larger than NeRF-based ones. This stands in stark contrast to NeRF-based methods, which efficiently model view-dependent effects through neural network conditioning with minimal parameter growth. Gaussian representations also tend to struggle to densify and optimize extremely distant objects, which often leaves the backgrounds of unbounded scenes blurry.\n\nThe large size of 3DGS models has motivated research into compact representations that preserve their performance advantages. Existing approaches either compress the per-Gaussian parameters, for example with vector quantization, typically trading some rendering quality for storage efficiency, or adopt hybrid neural-3DGS architectures in which neural components predict Gaussian properties instead of storing them explicitly, for instance anchor points carrying neural features that predict local Gaussian properties, or neural fields that store Gaussian properties directly. A natural way to reduce storage is thus to encode 3D Gaussian properties in grid-based neural fields. This, however, faces a fundamental limitation: the fixed resolution of grid-based representations struggles to capture the high-frequency spatial variations in 3D Gaussian properties. The issue is particularly pronounced in scenes with rapid opacity and scale changes at object boundaries or with high-frequency view-dependent effects, and naively fitting 3D Gaussians to neural fields often fails to reconstruct fine details such as thin geometric structures and high-frequency color variations. Moreover, querying neural networks to obtain the properties of large numbers of Gaussians adds computational overhead that can compromise real-time rendering.\n\nThe central problem is therefore how to design a scene representation that retains the real-time rendering speed and high visual quality of explicit 3D Gaussians while approaching the compactness of neural fields, without losing the high-frequency details that grid-based neural fields tend to miss. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth.           "questions": "Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a pivotal technique for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models on complex tasks. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), the language model is treated as a policy whose chain of thought is modeled as a sequence of actions, and it is optimized with rewards from an automatic verifier that compares the final answer extracted from each sampled solution with a reference answer. Most RLVR algorithms are on-policy; a widely used example is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward against a group of trajectories sampled for the same question. On-policy optimization is stable but computationally expensive, because the experience generated during the costly rollout phase is typically discarded after a single gradient update. This not only squanders substantial compute but also forfeits the opportunity for the model to learn from its own earlier successful explorations, which makes training inefficient, can make it unstable, and imposes a bottleneck on scaling RL for reasoning.\n\nExperience replay is a classical RL technique to address this issue: previously collected interactions are stored and reused, which improves sample efficiency, helps stabilize training and accelerates convergence, and prioritized variants emphasize the most informative transitions. It has been argued that AI is entering a period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement. A non-trivial challenge, however, lies in how to exploit past experiences according to their differing value and how to manage the replay process over the course of learning, and efficient experience replay mechanisms remain largely underexplored in RLVR for large reasoning models. Recent off-policy approaches incorporate historical or external data, for example by mixing expert demonstrations with on-policy updates or by deriving direct off-policy update rules, and recent replay methods for reasoning models reuse successful trajectories collected early in training or produced by a well-trained policy. However, the impact of the quality of the data within the replay buffer remains underexplored, and several replay methods do not correct for the distribution mismatch between the past policy that generated a stored trajectory and the current policy.\n\nSeveral features make the problem challenging. An experience in RLVR consists of a question together with the trajectories sampled for it, and it is unclear whether all questions are equally useful for training, or whether all successful trajectories for a question are equally worth reusing. Because the verifiable reward only checks the final answer, a successful trajectory may still rest on invalid reasoning. The usefulness of a stored experience may also change as the model's capabilities evolve during training. Finally, reusing past successes pushes the policy toward exploitation, while prior work shows that aggressively minimizing policy entropy can cause collapse, so the reuse of experience has to be balanced against continued exploration.\n\nThis raises the following research questions.           "questions": "Dictionary learning, in its most general form, assumes that observations X are generated by latent variables Z through an unknown function, X = g(Z). The goal is to recover the latent generative process from observational data alone, a fundamental task in both science and machine learning. This nonparametric formulation unifies a wide range of latent variable models, including independent component analysis, factor analysis and causal representation learning.\n\nIdentifiability, the ability to recover the true generative model from data, is crucial for understanding the hidden world. Yet in general dictionary learning, where both the latent variables and the generating process are unknown, the problem is fundamentally ill-posed without additional assumptions, akin to finding a needle in a haystack. To reduce this ambiguity, most prior work imposes strong parametric constraints that limit the space of possible solutions. The practice is so widespread that, although dictionary learning is fundamentally nonparametric, it is almost always instantiated as a linear model, in which observations are sparse linear combinations of latent variables. Such linearity can be overly restrictive and fails to capture the complexity of many real-world generative processes. Sparse autoencoders, commonly used in mechanistic interpretability, especially for foundation models, are a relevant example: although effective in some settings, they are rooted in sparse linear dictionary learning, which raises concerns about their ability to represent the inherently nonlinear structure of large-scale neural representations.\n\nMany efforts have been made to relax the linearity assumption. In nonlinear independent component analysis, one line of work leverages auxiliary variables as weak supervision to achieve identifiability under statistical independence, while another constrains the mixing function itself. In causal representation learning, identifiability often depends on access to interventional data or counterfactual views, which presuppose some control over the data-generating process. Some basic conditions cannot be avoided: just as linear dictionary learning needs conditions such as the restricted isometry property so that distinct latent codes map to distinguishable observations, the nonlinear generating function must be smooth and injective so that no information is lost. But avoiding information loss is not sufficient for full recovery of the latent variables in the nonlinear regime, which is why existing guarantees rely on restricted function classes or on auxiliary information such as domain or time indices, interventions or counterfactual data.\n\nA gap therefore remains between theoretical guarantees and practical utility. Theoretically, while additional assumptions can yield recovery guarantees, it is rarely possible to verify whether they hold in practice; understanding which guarantees remain valid when assumptions are violated is therefore essential for reliably uncovering the truth in general settings. Practically, what matters is less identifiability under ideal conditions than which inductive biases promote recovery, especially when the ground truth is unknown. Yet most existing approaches offer no guarantees under even mild violations of their assumptions, which makes their associated biases, such as contrastive objectives or weak supervision, difficult to generalize across settings.\n\nThe challenge is to make identifiability actionable in general settings: only observational data are available, the generating function is nonlinear and unknown, no parametric constraint or auxiliary supervision can be relied upon, and only basic conditions such as invertibility and differentiability are assumed, accepting that recovering every latent variable may then be infeasible. In such settings, two questions remain open:\n- What aspects of the latent process can still be recovered with guarantees?\n- What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery, ideally ones that could be adopted universally across models and settings?\nA related question is whether, and under which additional conditions that require no auxiliary information, all latent variables could still be recovered.",

          "questions": "Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.\n\nA second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.\n\nMultimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task.           "questions": "Humans naturally parse scenes into coherent objects (e.g., grouping features such as a rounded shape, a smooth surface and a muted color into the mug) and further ground their identities in context (e.g., recognizing my coffee mug on the desk rather than just a mug). This is assumed to be made possible by what cognitive scientists call object binding, the brain's ability to group an object's low-level features (color, shape, motion, etc.) into a unified representation. This in turn enables objects to be stored efficiently and compositionally in memory and used as high-level symbols for reasoning about individual object instances. The binding problem is a genuine computational challenge, as evidenced by humans' limited competence in conjunction-search tasks and by clinical dissociations such as Balint's syndrome, where feature perception remains intact but binding breaks down. If AI systems could replicate the human ability for object binding, that may help them ground symbols in perception and exploit compositionality. The key question is: do current AI systems solve the binding problem?\n\nObject binding has received little attention in mainstream AI research. Cognition-inspired models build in human-like object-based attention. By contrast, mainstream vision models are assumed to learn implicitly to handle multiple objects from training data, yet empirical studies show that they often \"attend\" only to the most salient regions and overlook the rest. While the attention scores of Vision Transformers (ViTs) can capture global image structure and salient regions (often corresponding to target objects), empirical evidence shows that self-attention tends to group patches by low-level feature similarity rather than reliably producing object-level binding. Object-centric methods such as Slot Attention fix this by allocating a small set of learnable slots that compete for token features, enforcing binding by design; however, because such modules are added externally rather than integrated into the transformer architecture, they introduce additional challenges for scaling and training. Other work has assumed that ViTs already carry implicit object-level structure and has tried to group patches into objects directly from their activations or attention maps. Binding failures are also seen as a source of performance breakdowns in modern transformer-based systems: text-to-image diffusion models suffer attribute leakage between entities (e.g., both a dog and a cat end up wearing sunglasses and a sun-hat), and vision-language models struggle to differentiate multiple objects defined by feature conjunctions. Despite these failures, transformers still demonstrate some binding capability, yet the underlying mechanism is not well understood: binding has started to be characterized in language models, but binding mechanisms in vision transformers remain unexplored. Whether AI vision models, especially leading ViTs, can achieve robust object binding without explicit mechanisms therefore remains an open question.\n\nCognitive scientists have questioned whether ViTs can bind objects at all, arguing that they lack mechanisms for dynamically and flexibly grouping features, that they lack the recurrence necessary for iterative refinement of object representations, and that, as purely connectionist models, they appear incapable of true symbolic processing. However, these architectural limitations do not preclude binding from emerging through learning. ViTs share several computational parallels with the mammalian visual system: both rely on parallel, distributed and hierarchical processing; explicit position embeddings resemble the spatial tagging and spatiotopic organization observed in the ventral stream; and self-attention is akin to the dynamic tuning and attentional modulation thought to be primary mechanisms of binding in the brain. Moreover, knowing which patches belong to the same object would be useful for prediction and could guide attention, and human-labeled data also reflects object-level structure, so ViTs could acquire binding by imitation. ViTs may therefore learn to bind objects directly from large-scale training data, without requiring explicit architectural inductive biases.\n\nThis raises the question of whether object binding naturally emerges in large, pretrained Vision Transformers, a question that matters for both cognitive science and AI. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.\n\nTraditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.\n\nA growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. OOD detection seeks to identify such inputs and is critical for reliable deployment in open-world scenarios, including safety-critical applications and scientific discovery tasks. The challenge becomes even more pronounced for graph-structured data, because of their non-Euclidean nature and complex topological structures.\n\nRecent advances in graph-level OOD detection fall broadly into two categories. End-to-end methods train OOD-specific graph neural networks (GNNs) from scratch using only unlabeled in-distribution (ID) data; they typically rely on unsupervised objectives such as graph contrastive learning to extract discriminative representations that can separate ID and OOD samples during inference. Post-hoc methods instead start from well-trained GNNs and fine-tune OOD detectors that refine the predictions or representations at inference time. Among them, a recent test-time method, GOODAT, directly optimizes a learnable graph masker on the test samples without altering the pre-trained model. This test-time setting with data-centric modification is more practical, because it removes the dependency on labeled training data and on model retraining.\n\nThe test-time problem can be stated as follows. A GNN has been pre-trained on graphs from an unlabeled ID dataset. At test time it faces unlabeled graphs that mix held-out ID graphs, disjoint from the pre-training graphs, with graphs drawn from a different, OOD distribution. The goal is a detector that assigns each test graph a score, a higher score meaning a greater probability that the graph comes from the OOD distribution, using only the pre-trained model and the test graphs: the parameters of the pre-trained model are not modified, and neither the training data nor any ground-truth label is used.\n\nDespite the progress of this data-centric paradigm, a less-explored challenge persists. A pre-trained model can effectively extract information from ID data, but when it infers on both ID and OOD test graphs it lacks ground-truth information indicative of the underlying distribution, information that is often embedded within the graph structure. Test graphs typically comprise distinctive components, whose capture could intuitively differentiate OOD samples from ID graphs, together with irrelevant structural elements. The pervasive presence of similar irrelevant structural elements in ID and OOD graphs, a structural redundancy that induces semantic shifts, hinders current methods from accurately capturing and distinguishing the essential structures of ID and OOD data. The existing test-time method tries to address this concern by using graph maskers to identify subgraphs in the test data that are similar to those in the ID training graphs, but it fundamentally relies on learnable graph augmentations, which can inadvertently alter the semantic information of substructures or lead to information loss, thereby compromising the reliability of OOD detection.\n\nThis raises the following questions.           "questions": "Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning (SciML). Among the most promising approaches are operator-learning architectures, particularly the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) and its variants. These models leverage mesh-independent spectral convolutions to efficiently capture fine-scale dynamics in the frequency domain, enabling orders-of-magnitude faster inference than traditional numerical solvers. Recently, the field has seen the rise of Large Operator Models (LOMs), which scale these architectures and employ large-scale pre-training on diverse datasets, unlocking remarkable generalization capabilities for complex downstream tasks. A rapidly growing body of work now treats such models as foundation models: they are first pre-trained on heterogeneous collections of PDEs and later adapted to new physical regimes, with recent models scaling to around one billion parameters.\n\nWhen adapting large pre-trained models to downstream tasks, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a powerful strategy, offering minimal computational and storage overhead. Unlike full-model fine-tuning, PEFT techniques train only a small subset of parameters, which preserves the benefits of pre-training while enabling rapid deployment across tasks and domains. Many such techniques exist, ranging from learned soft prompts and small bottleneck modules inserted between layers to low-rank updates of frozen weight matrices, such as LoRA, and its numerous variants; together they show how structural priors can drastically reduce the number of trainable parameters while retaining fine-tuning flexibility. This paradigm has proven highly effective in natural language processing and computer vision, where large foundation models dominate and efficient task adaptation is critical for scalability.\n\nHowever, the potential of PEFT within SciML remains unexplored. Although a few recent studies employ LoRA-style physics-informed neural networks to build surrogates for parameterized PDEs, they train modest networks from scratch on small, single-type equation datasets, so a systematic study of PEFT for pre-trained LOMs has yet to be established.           "questions": "The multi-objective multi-armed bandit problem generalizes the classical, single-objective multi-armed bandit to settings with multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Pulling an arm yields a vector of objective-specific rewards, so a single \"best\" arm is often ill-defined and optimality must account for trade-offs across objectives. The setting of interest here is the multi-objective linear contextual bandit: at each round, every arm of a finite set is described by a d-dimensional context vector, which may be chosen adversarially; each of the L objectives has its own fixed but unknown parameter vector; and the agent, after choosing an arm, observes an L-dimensional reward vector whose entry for each objective is the inner product of the arm's context with that objective's parameter, plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise.\n\nOne simple way to handle trade-offs is scalarization, which maps reward vectors to a scalar via, for example, weighted sums, minimax, or other nonlinear transforms, thereby reducing the problem to a single-objective bandit. However, selecting a suitable scalarization is itself nontrivial, and an arm that is optimal under one scalarization can be markedly suboptimal under another. An alternative is to reason directly in the vector space via Pareto optimality: the Pareto front comprises the arms whose mean reward vectors are not dominated component-wise by that of any other arm. Because it compares reward vectors objective-wise, Pareto optimality is more general than committing to a fixed scalarization. Performance is then usually measured by the Pareto regret, which sums over rounds the smallest uniform increase that would make the mean reward vector of the chosen arm non-dominated.\n\nPrior work on Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits proposes and studies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, which typically compute an empirical Pareto front at every round and are therefore complex. Approaches that identify the Pareto front by eliminating arms do not carry over to the contextual setting, where the Pareto front changes with the contexts and an arm discarded early may later be Pareto optimal. By contrast, the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling has not been studied for multi-objective bandits: the only Thompson Sampling algorithm proposed for this problem comes without theoretical analysis, and the analyses of randomized scalarization in multi-objective Bayesian optimization concern the Bayesian regret under a known Gaussian prior, with bounds that increase with the number of objectives. This gap is noteworthy: in many single-objective contextual and non-contextual bandits, Thompson Sampling and its variants are empirically competitive with or superior to UCB methods, yet their worst-case (frequentist) analyses are typically more delicate. Extending Thompson Sampling to several objectives introduces additional challenges, including coordinating randomized samples across multiple objectives, ensuring optimism of the randomized estimates across all objectives simultaneously, and handling the possibility of multiple Pareto-optimal arms.\n\nA second issue concerns the performance measure itself. The standard Pareto regret compares per-round mean reward vectors; consequently, a policy that plays only Pareto-optimal arms incurs zero Pareto regret, even when an alternative selection of arms over the same number of rounds would yield strictly larger cumulative rewards in every objective. Pareto regret therefore does not distinguish between policies that obtain different cumulative rewards while selecting only Pareto-optimal arms, and the resulting shortfall can grow with the number of rounds.\n\nThis raises two questions. First, can a computationally efficient, Thompson Sampling-type randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit be designed with worst-case Pareto regret guarantees, how close can these guarantees come to those known for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, and how must they depend on the number of objectives? Second, how should optimality and regret be defined in this setting so that they also account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections, penalizing policies that are Pareto optimal round by round but inefficient in aggregate?",

          "questions": "Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.\n\nCurrent UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.\n\nA compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata.
